In '86. Never perturbed', what is the primary Dhamma theme and practical guidance offered?

In '86. Never perturbed', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Never perturbed]
It was after 10 p.m., and I saw that Luang Pu was sitting and resting, so I went to inform him, “Luang Pu, Ajaan Khao has died.”
Instead of asking when or how, Luang Pu said,
“Ah, yes."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as an external philosophy, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text emphasizes, the Dhamma is *akāliko* (timeless) and *opanayiko* (leading inward), realizable (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner through patient, honest awareness.

Never perturbed', kamma is discussed in this context: *"But as for bad karma associated with the body, even noble ones—no matter what the level of their attainment—still have to contend with these things until they’re finally released from them and no longer involved with them."* Here, kamma (kamma — volitional action shaping future experience) is treated not as a theoretical doctrine, but as a living faculty to be actively cultivated and observed. When we bring genuine mindfulness to our direct experience, the quality of kamma helps dismantle habitual delusion and stabilizes the mind in clear, unentangled awareness.

The text reflects: *"But as for bad karma associated with the body, even noble ones—no matter what the level of their attainment—still have to contend with these things until they’re finally released from them and no longer involved with them."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.

How does '86. Never perturbed' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"The normal state of the mind is that it has to live with things of this sort."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.
